**Downsampling changes the class prior seen during training.** If positives are rare but most negatives are removed, a model can learn useful separation while reporting probabilities appropriate to the artificially balanced sample. Those probabilities are too high for the original population unless corrected under suitable assumptions. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html)

**Use odds to see the correction.** Let sampled-model probability be s, sampled positive prior be $\pi_s$, and true prior be $\pi$. If sampling depends only on class and class-conditional feature distributions are unchanged, population odds equal sampled odds multiplied by $[\pi/(1-\pi)]/[\pi_s/(1-\pi_s)]$. Convert the corrected odds back to a probability by dividing by one plus the odds.

If all positives are retained and each negative is retained with probability 0.01, the odds multiplier is 0.01. A sampled prediction of 0.5 has odds one; corrected odds are 0.01, giving probability about 0.0099—not 0.5.

**The assumptions are essential.** If negatives are selected based on features or hardness, a single prior correction is generally insufficient. The model must also be reasonably calibrated for the sampled distribution; the formula cannot repair arbitrary model error.

Evaluate calibration on representative untouched population data, and keep ranking versus probability estimation distinct. Downsampling can save training work, but thresholds and expected-cost decisions must use the appropriate population probabilities or otherwise account for the altered sampling design.

**Technical details and references.**

Assume sampling changes only class priors, retaining the same class-conditional feature distributions. Let $p_s$ be the model probability under sampled prior $\pi_s$ and let population prior be $\pi$. Correct the odds by the prior-odds ratio. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/calibration.html) [2](https://probml.github.io/pml-book/book1.html)

$$a=\frac{\pi(1-\pi_s)}{(1-\pi)\pi_s},\qquad p=\frac{ap_s}{1-p_s+ap_s}.$$

If all positives are retained and negatives have retention $r=0.01$, then $a=r$. A sampled-model probability 0.5 becomes $0.01/1.01\approx0.009901$. The correction assumes the sampled-model scores are calibrated and sampling is independent of features within class. Feature-dependent sampling, prior drift, and model misspecification require more than this adjustment. Choose decision thresholds using population costs and prevalence.
